note: Most of this war was fought without front lines, so areas are drawn only for well-documented North Vietnamese gains (Hue in 1968, the 1972 Easter Offensive and the 1975 offensive), hand-drawn from campaign maps and approximate; guerrilla control of the countryside is not mapped.

chapters.title: The Gulf of Tonkin and escalation
arrows: US Marines land at Da Nang
chapters.text: Vietnam had been divided since 1954, and by 1964 the communist Viet Cong, backed by North Vietnam, were winning the war in the South's countryside. On 2 August 1964 North Vietnamese boats clashed with the US destroyer Maddox in the Gulf of Tonkin; a second attack reported on 4 August did not happen, but Congress gave President Johnson power to wage war. Bombing of the North (Operation Rolling Thunder) began in March 1965, US Marines landed at Da Nang on 8 March, and by July Johnson had committed large ground forces. Guerrilla control was patchy and is not mapped.

chapters.title: Ia Drang
arrows: North Vietnamese attack on Plei Me
US air assault into the Ia Drang valley
chapters.text: In October 1965 North Vietnamese regiments besieged the Special Forces camp at Plei Me in the Central Highlands. The new US 1st Cavalry Division, moving by helicopter, pursued them west towards the Cambodian border, and from 14 to 18 November fought the first major battle between US and North Vietnamese army units in the Ia Drang valley. Both sides claimed success, and both drew lessons: the US relied on helicopters and firepower, while the North Vietnamese learned to fight at close quarters.

chapters.title: The Tet Offensive
arrows: US and South Vietnamese counter-attack in Hue
chapters.text: On 30–31 January 1968, during the Tet holiday truce, the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese attacked more than 100 towns and cities across the South, including the US embassy in Saigon, while the Marine base at Khe Sanh was under siege. Most attacks were beaten back within days, but communist troops held much of Hue until its Citadel was retaken on 24 February, and thousands of civilians were killed there. The attackers suffered huge losses, yet the offensive turned American opinion against the war.

chapters.title: Into Cambodia and Laos
arrows: South Vietnamese incursion into the Parrot's Beak
Lam Son 719: South Vietnamese drive on Tchepone
chapters.text: North Vietnamese troops and supplies moved along the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and used base areas in eastern Cambodia. After Cambodia's neutral leader Sihanouk was overthrown in March 1970, US and South Vietnamese forces struck these sanctuaries between 29 April and 22 July. In February–March 1971, without US ground troops, South Vietnamese forces drove into Laos along Route 9 to Tchepone (Lam Son 719) but were forced back with heavy losses. Control of the Laotian and Cambodian borderlands is not mapped.

chapters.title: The Easter Offensive
arrows: North Vietnamese offensive across the DMZ
North Vietnamese offensive in Binh Long
North Vietnamese offensive in the Central Highlands
South Vietnamese counter-offensive at Quang Tri
chapters.text: With most US troops gone, North Vietnam launched a conventional invasion on 30 March 1972 with tanks and artillery on three fronts. In the north it took Dong Ha and, on 1 May, Quang Tri city; in the west it took Loc Ninh and Dak To but was held at An Loc and Kontum, helped by massive US air power. South Vietnamese Marines and paratroopers retook Quang Tri city on 16 September, but the North kept much of the ground it had won.

chapters.title: The Paris Peace Accords
chapters.text: The Paris Peace Accords, signed on 27 January 1973, called for a ceasefire in place and the withdrawal of US forces, and the last US combat troops left at the end of March. North Vietnamese troops were allowed to stay where they were in the South, so the ceasefire left a patchwork of areas, many of them only villages and jungle, that cannot be mapped exactly. Fighting soon resumed.

chapters.title: The Highlands and the coast fall
arrows: South Vietnamese retreat from the Highlands
Advance on Hue and Da Nang
chapters.text: Phuoc Long province fell on 6 January 1975 and the US did not respond. On 10–11 March North Vietnamese forces took Ban Me Thuot; President Thieu ordered the Highlands abandoned, and the retreating columns were destroyed on the road to the coast. Hue fell on 25–26 March and Da Nang on 29–30 March amid panic, and within days the cities of the central coast, from Qui Nhon to Nha Trang and Cam Ranh, had fallen too.

chapters.title: Xuan Loc and the fall of Saigon
arrows: Final assault on Saigon from the east
Final assault on Saigon from the north-west
chapters.text: At Xuan Loc, 60 km east of Saigon, South Vietnamese troops held out from 9 to 21 April before withdrawing; Phan Rang fell on 16 April. As North Vietnamese divisions closed in, the US evacuated its last citizens and thousands of Vietnamese by helicopter. On 30 April tanks broke through the gates of the Independence Palace in Saigon and the South surrendered, ending the war; Vietnam was formally reunified in 1976.
